title: Vocabulary: precise language for Writing Task 2 arguments
status: Owner approved v1.0.0 on 2026-10-26; teacher release to all eligible schools (optional vocabulary lesson)
rights: Original Brains Heist LLC instructional material, AI-assisted. Passages, people and data are fictional and created for practice. Not official IELTS material. Human editorial and classroom review recommended.
prerequisites: Learners can identify the question type in a Task 2 prompt.
Optional vocabulary lesson: use when essays rely on 'good/bad', 'very' and 'I think' or overstate claims.

objectives.text: Express a clear position and qualify claims precisely (arguably, to some extent, it is likely that).
Use cause, effect and solution collocations accurately (lead to, stem from, tackle a problem, address the issue).
Replace vague words (good, bad, a lot, thing) with precise, natural alternatives.

levels.foundation: Use the six cause/effect/solution phrases in model sentences before writing your own.
levels.core: Write the paragraph with no use of 'good', 'bad', 'thing' or 'a lot of'.
levels.extension: Qualify one claim with hedging and support it with a specific example.
levels.high_band: Write a full body paragraph that concedes a counter-argument and rebuts it, using three word-bank items naturally.

word_bank.example: Long working hours can lead to stress.
Many health problems stem from poor diet.

word_bank.meaning: take action to deal with a problem

word_bank.example: Noise has a detrimental effect on concentration.
Exercise is beneficial to mental health.

word_bank.meaning: it can be argued (a careful claim)
word_bank.example: Arguably, the internet is the most important invention of the century.

word_bank.item: to some extent / to a large extent
word_bank.example: I agree with this view to a large extent.
It is unlikely that cars will disappear soon.

word_bank.meaning: many / a large part of (more precise than 'a lot of')
word_bank.example: A significant proportion of graduates work abroad.

word_bank.item: a key factor / a major concern
word_bank.example: Cost is a key factor in this decision.
One drawback of online learning is isolation.

word_bank.meaning: accept a point, then argue against it

stages.title: Opening challenge: vague or precise?
stages.student: Decide which sentence an examiner would reward most.
stages.teacher: Learners vote; reveal comments. Focus on precision, not long words.
stages.say: Precise words make an argument clearer, not just longer.
stages.check: Learners can name two vague words in Learner A's sentence.

stages.title: Word bank: cause, effect, solution and stance
stages.student: Group the word bank: cause/effect, solutions, stance and concession. Note the preposition after each item.
stages.teacher: Drill the prepositions: lead to, stem from, beneficial to, a detrimental effect on.
stages.say: The preposition is part of the word.
stages.check: Learners complete five items with the right preposition.

stages.title: Collocations and prepositions
stages.student: Complete each sentence with ONE word.
stages.teacher: Seven minutes, bank closed for core and above.
stages.say: Check the word and the word after it.
stages.check: Most learners score six or more.

stages.title: Upgrade the vague sentence
stages.student: Choose the most precise and natural version.
stages.teacher: Discuss why over-formal or wrong-collocation options fail.
stages.say: Natural and accurate beats rare and wrong.
stages.check: Learners explain one wrong option per question.

stages.title: Plan a body paragraph
stages.student: Plan: topic sentence, cause, effect, example, solution.
stages.teacher: Check that each plan has a specific example.
stages.check: Every learner has a plan with an example.

stages.title: Write independently
stages.student: Write one body paragraph using at least five word-bank items.
stages.say: Underline each word-bank item you use.

stages.title: Compare with the model
stages.student: Find the cause/effect and hedging language in the model; improve two phrases in your own paragraph.
stages.teacher: Ask learners to read one improved sentence aloud.
stages.say: The model is illustrative, not a target band.

stages.title: Exit ticket and homework
stages.student: Complete the exit ticket and note the homework.
stages.say: Keep a list of the vague words you over-use and their replacements.
stages.check: Every learner writes one hedged claim.

blocks.title: Vague or precise?
blocks.mode: Opening challenge; learners decide before the reveal
blocks.instructions: Question: 'Many people work long hours. What problems does this cause?' Three learners wrote a sentence. Which is best?

examples.label: Learner A
examples.text: Working a lot is a bad thing because it causes a lot of problems for people.
examples.comment: Vague: 'a lot', 'bad thing' and 'problems' say nothing specific.

examples.label: Learner B
examples.text: Excessive working hours can lead to chronic stress, which in turn has a detrimental effect on family relationships.
examples.comment: Best: precise words, a clear cause and effect, and careful 'can'.

examples.label: Learner C
examples.text: Long hours of labour engender multitudinous deleterious ramifications.
examples.comment: Over-formal and unnatural; the examiner rewards accurate, natural vocabulary, not rare words used to impress.

blocks.title: Collocations and prepositions
blocks.mode: Controlled practice; word bank closed for core and above
blocks.instructions: Complete each sentence with ONE word.

items.prompt: Poor air quality can ______ to breathing difficulties in children.
Many traffic problems stem ______ a lack of public transport.
Regular exercise is beneficial ______ both physical and mental health.
Excessive screen time may have a detrimental effect ______ sleep.
Governments need to ______ the problem of youth unemployment.
In my view, the advantages of studying abroad ______ the disadvantages.
I agree with this statement to a large ______.
The city council could ______ a ban on cars in the historic centre.

blocks.title: Upgrade the vague sentence
blocks.instructions: Choose the most precise and natural version, A, B or C.

items.prompt: 'A lot of students have money problems.'
items.evidence: a significant number of + financial difficulties
items.reason: A is wrong collocation; C overclaims.
options: A  A big amount of students have money problems.
B  A significant number of students experience financial difficulties.
C  Every student suffers from extreme poverty.

items.prompt: 'Technology is good for education.'
items.reason: A is unnatural; B is still vague.
options: A  Technology is very goodly for education.
B  Technology is a nice thing in education.
C  Technology can be beneficial to learning, for example by giving students access to online resources.

items.prompt: 'Online shopping will kill all small shops.'
items.reason: B overclaims; C changes the meaning.
options: A  Online shopping is likely to force a significant number of small shops to close.
B  Online shopping will definitely destroy every shop in the world.
C  Online shopping is beneficial to small shops.

items.prompt: 'There are bad things about working from home.'
items.reason: A is still vague; C wrong word form.
options: A  Working from home has some bad sides.
B  Working from home has certain drawbacks, such as isolation from colleagues.
C  Working from home has disadvantageous.

items.prompt: 'Some people say fees are too high, but universities need money.'
items.reason: A loses the contrast; B wrong linker.
options: A  Fees are high and universities need money.
B  Fees are high, therefore universities need money.
C  Admittedly, tuition fees are high; however, universities require funding to maintain standards.

items.prompt: 'Pollution is a big problem in cities.'
items.reason: B and C are vague or wrong collocations.
options: A  Air pollution has become a major concern in many large cities.
B  Pollution is a very big huge problem.
C  Pollution makes a big problem to cities.

blocks.title: One developed body paragraph
blocks.mode: Independent classroom application after modelling; not a full Task 2 or Writing Screener
blocks.prompt: In many countries, young people spend several hours a day on social media. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to reduce them? Write ONE body paragraph (about 120-150 words) about EITHER the problems OR the solutions.
blocks.conditions: 13 minutes, independent. No model visible. Record word-bank use.
blocks.support: Frame: topic sentence → cause/effect (lead to, have a detrimental effect on) → specific example → link back. Solutions: tackle, introduce, it is likely that.
blocks.extension: Add a hedged claim (arguably / it is likely that).
blocks.high_band: Concede one counter-point with 'admittedly' and rebut it.
blocks.model_label: Illustrative classroom model for discussion only. Not a certified band answer.
blocks.model: The most serious problem associated with heavy social media use is arguably its effect on young people's mental health. Constant exposure to carefully edited images of other people's lives can lead to unrealistic comparisons, and a significant proportion of teenagers report feeling anxious or inadequate as a result. Excessive use late at night also has a detrimental effect on sleep, which in turn makes it harder to concentrate at school. For example, a student who checks messages until midnight is unlikely to perform well in a morning examination. Admittedly, social media allows young people to stay in touch with friends; however, these benefits are unlikely to outweigh the harm when use becomes compulsive. It is therefore a major concern that parents and schools should not ignore.
checklist: Lexical Resource: Have you replaced vague words (good, bad, thing, a lot of)?
Lexical Resource: Are prepositions correct (lead to, stem from, effect on)?
Task Response: Is there a specific example that supports the main idea?
Coherence and Cohesion: Does the paragraph develop one idea from topic sentence to conclusion?

blocks.title: Homework: replace the vague words
blocks.mode: Homework; checked at the start of the next lesson
blocks.instructions: Write a more precise word or phrase (no more than FOUR words) to replace the words in brackets.

items.prompt: Cheap flights have [made happen] a rise in tourism.
[A lot of] young adults now live with their parents.
items.reason: Also: many, a large proportion of.

items.prompt: Fast food is [bad for] children's health.
The government should [do something about] homelessness.
Learning a language is [good for] the brain.
One [bad point] of city life is noise.

exit_ticket: Two phrases for cause and effect, with their prepositions:
A vague word I will stop using, and my replacement:
homework: Complete the vague-word replacements on the homework sheet.
Rewrite the conclusion of your last Task 2 essay, replacing every vague word with a precise one.
delayed_followup: In Lesson 15 (Task 2 under time), check whether essays use precise cause/effect collocations and hedging. Record it as a later observation.

blocks.title: Fresh check: precise argument language
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-4: complete each sentence with ONE word. Questions 5-6: choose the best version, A, B or C.

items.prompt: Rising house prices have resulted ______ more young people renting.
Many cases of obesity are ______ by a lack of physical activity.
Local authorities could ______ stricter recycling rules.
In my opinion, the risks of genetic testing do not ______ its benefits.
'Tourism is bad for old cities.'
options: A  Tourism is a bad thing for old cities.
B  Mass tourism can have a detrimental effect on historic city centres, for instance through overcrowding.
C  Tourism makes a detrimental to old cities.

items.prompt: 'Some say robots will take all jobs, but this is wrong.'
items.reason: A overclaims; B loses the contrast.
options: A  Robots will never take any jobs at all.
B  Robots will take jobs and people will lose work.
C  Admittedly, automation will replace some jobs; however, it is unlikely to eliminate human work entirely.
